title: Vedic Society, Polity and Economy

cards.b: The Vedic age sits between the Harappans and the Mahajanapadas. You need to tell Early and Later Vedic apart. Questions mix texts, society, polity and the economy.

The Rig Veda (earliest, c. 1500 to 1000 BCE) and later Vedas (Sama, Yajur, Atharva), Brahmanas, Aranyakas and Upanishads (c. 1000 to 600 BCE). Archaeology: Painted Grey Ware (PGW) culture in the Ganga-Yamuna doab links to Later Vedic. The Aryans’ origin is a debate (see below). Vedanga and Sutra texts followed.

Saptasindhu region. Society: tribal (jana); family (kula); the rajan was a tribal chief, assisted by the purohita (Vashishtha, Vishvamitra) and senani. Assemblies: Sabha, Samiti, Vidatha, Gana. Economy: cattle (gau, gavishthi for war), pastoralism, limited agriculture; nishka as ornament, barter. Gods: Indra (war), Agni, Varuna, Soma. Women: Ghosha, Lopamudra, Apala; the Dasarajna battle (ten kings) on the Parushni (Ravi). Varna mentioned only in the Purusha Sukta, a late hymn.

Shift east to the Ganga-Yamuna doab and Kosala-Kashi (c. 1000 to 600 BCE). Larger kingdoms (janapadas): Kuru, Panchala. Rulers performed Rajasuya, Ashvamedha, Vajapeya. The Sabha and Samiti declined; the kingdom grew with bali (tax) and sangrihitri (treasurer). Society: four varnas firmly formed; ashrama system (Brahmacharya, Grihastha, Vanaprastha, Sanyasa); gotra. Women lost status somewhat.

Agriculture became main: iron (shyama ayas, krishna ayas; iron from about 1000 to 800 BCE at sites such as Atranjikhera), plough, rice (vrihi), wheat, barley; sali. Crafts: carpenters, smiths, potters, weavers; trade; nishka and satamana as proto-currency; PGW and NBPW pottery. Cities emerged only later, around 600 BCE.

Early: nature gods and sacrifices (yajna), no temples. Later: ritual complexity, priestly power (Brahmanas); Prajapati, Vishnu and Rudra rose; Indra declined. Upanishads: Brahman and Atman, karma, moksha; “Satyameva Jayate” from the Mundaka Upanishad. Ritual debates gave rise to Buddhism and Jainism.

The Ramayana and the Mahabharata took their form between about 400 BCE and 400 CE. Dharmasutras (Gautama, Apastamba) and later Manusmriti (c. 200 BCE to 200 CE) set social and legal norms. These are used with caution, as they are composite texts.

Max Müller (1850s) proposed Aryan migration from Central Asia. Indian writers (B. G. Tilak: Arctic home; others: Indian origin) argued differently. Linguists point to Indo-European roots. Genetics (Narasimhan et al. 2019; Shinde et al. 2019) show steppe ancestry in many South Asians after 2000 BCE. Historians such as Romila Thapar stress that “Aryan” is a linguistic term, not a race. The debate remains charged.

The Mundaka line “Satyameva Jayate” is India’s national motto. Sabha and Samiti are cited in discussions of Indian democratic roots; the Lok Sabha and Parliament use these words. The ashrama and varna ideas remain in social debates. Yajna and Vedic chanting are on UNESCO’s ICH list (Vedic chanting, 2008).
